articles.title: They Suffered Brain Injuries After Riding a Six Flags Roller Coaster. Regulators Pinned the Blame on Them.
articles.author: Joe Rubin
paras: A 17-year-old boy died after riding the extreme X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California this summer, just weeks before two more people suffered severe brain injuries after riding the same attraction, ProPublica and L.A. Material have found.

A homicide detective investigating Christopher Gibson’s death in June sent an email to the California official responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety. But records show that the official did not reply until nearly two months later. The lack of action raises the question of whether the brain damage suffered by the two riders the following month could have been avoided.
Christopher’s death, which has not been previously reported, also raises questions about Six Flags, its flagship X2 ride and the way in which California regulates roller coasters.

Billed as a “fourth-dimension” roller coaster, the X2 drew more than 16 million riders attracted to extreme thrills. It featured seats that swiveled in all directions as the ride hurtled and twisted along the track, sometimes at a rate of up to 76 mph.

The X2 was shut down temporarily after two separate brain hemorrhages in July. In August, CNN reported that the X2 had been “linked to more than a dozen reports of serious injuries” and two deaths over nearly two decades.

A ProPublica and L.A. Material investigation has found that state regulators have repeatedly failed to take swift action in the face of reported deaths and head injuries on the X2. On at least 70 occasions since 2010, Magic Mountain reported head injuries to the little-known unit within the California Division of Occupational Safety and Health responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety.

But rather than responding to those reports with vigorous inspections or safety checks, the regulators often did minimal or no investigation, according to a ProPublica and L.A. Material analysis of court filings, public records and internal regulatory documents.

“How many more people have to die before you think, ‘Well, maybe we should look at that?’” said Mariusz Ziejewski, a biomechanical engineer who has worked with the military to reduce brain injuries and was an expert witness in a lawsuit against Magic Mountain. “I think one is already way too much.”

CalOSHA and Magic Mountain instead frequently blamed riders for their injuries and in more than 35 cases alleged that people had somehow ridden the attraction incorrectly by failing to hold their heads in the right position. In one case, when a 14-year-old was hospitalized last year after losing consciousness on the ride, officials attributed it to the teenager’s menstrual cycle.

Six Flags and CalOSHA did not respond to detailed questions from ProPublica and L.A. Material. However, Denisse Gómez, a spokesperson for the state department that oversees CalOSHA, said in a statement that when theme park injuries are reported, regulators evaluate whether the ride was operating correctly and according to state safety rules. The agency is “committed to public safety,” she said, adding that “because that investigation is ongoing, we are not commenting on matters involving X2 at this time.”

Six Flags provided a statement that noted that the X2 had consistently passed safety tests, and its parks undergo preventative maintenance and a comprehensive, third-party inspection program. They also said their investigation of the ride remains ongoing, and that they are fully cooperating with CalOSHA. “Safety is our ethos and is at the heart of everything we do,” a spokesperson said.

When Six Flags has been sued for wrongful death or injuries related to the X2, it has maintained that injuries are rare and the ride is highly regulated by CalOSHA. In a recently settled lawsuit related to 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding the X2 in 2022, Magic Mountain’s director of public safety said in a declaration that the state has never notified the park of any “patron safety-related concerns related to the acceleration forces on the X2.”
Christopher Gibson was an autistic but healthy teen when he and his mother, Leanndra Fascaldo, drove from their Colorado home to California to celebrate his high school graduation at Magic Mountain.

The pair rode roller coasters for several days starting on May 31, including the X2 and the Viper, which Christopher called a “neck breaker,” according to a sheriff’s report. On their fourth day at the theme park, the teen once again rode the X2 and then the Great American Revolution before complaining of a headache. By early afternoon, they returned to the hotel.

That night, the pain grew worse. His mother gave him Advil. Eventually, he moved to the hotel room’s closet, where it was darker, and went back to sleep. His mother assumed he was just exhausted, but around 2 p.m. the next day she noticed that he had stopped snoring. She looked into the closet and saw that his lips were blue and his face was covered with “white and pink foam.” She called 911. Paramedics pronounced him dead at 3:16 p.m. on June 4.

Within a month, a sheriff’s homicide detective reached out to the California state office that regulates roller coasters, writing that “it is possible that he suffered an injury during his visits to the theme park.” The detective did not receive a reply until she contacted the office again two months later.

It’s been a deadly year for Six Flags. In addition to the California incident, an Atlanta school worker died in October after riding one of the theme park’s “hypercoasters” at Six Flags Over Georgia, prompting the company to temporarily close nine attractions at six theme parks across North America.

Theme park rides are regulated by states, not the federal government. In 2000, the legislature gave CalOSHA, the agency responsible for worker safety in California, oversight of roller coasters. Millions of people flock to the state’s theme parks each year, and the move came after a series of high-profile accidents in the 1990s. Under the law, state officials were given new power to conduct annual inspections, and theme parks must report accidents that result in serious injury to the agency.
But ProPublica and L.A. Material found that officials in CalOSHA’s Amusement Ride and Tramway Unit have frequently determined that investigations are unnecessary when accidents happen on the X2.

In 16 instances involving people who wound up in the hospital after riding the X2 between 2009 and 2022, CalOSHA invoked identical or similar language after checking a box on accident reports that said state action was not called for. “At this time, this accident does not warrant an investigation,” said one typical form. “The condition which developed while the patron was riding does not appear to be related to the maintenance or operation of the ride.” The report was filed in response to a woman who was hospitalized in 2016 with a head injury after riding the X2.

This also held true in cases where people lost their lives. When Hilda Farias suffered a massive brain hemorrhage after riding the X2 in October 2010, CalOSHA officials adopted similar language and conducted no inspection. The state regulator’s report did not even note that the 28-year-old mother of a 5-year-old had died, according to records obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material. Farias’ family sued the theme park, and the case settled in 2015.

When Hawley died in June 2022 after riding the X2, Magic Mountain initially told CalOSHA that the cause appeared to be heatstroke, according to a state report. The coroner later determined that Hawley, like Farias, had died of a massive brain hemorrhage. On that occasion, CalOSHA shut the ride down briefly while Six Flags conducted tests to measure the impact of g-forces on the rider and examined maintenance records. It ultimately determined that the ride was operating normally, according to a CalOSHA inspection obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material.
Christopher Gibson wore a Batman hoodie to school almost every day.

Diagnosed with autism when he was 5 or 6, Christopher was “high-functioning and verbal,” his mother told a sheriff’s detective. He had recently graduated high school and was headed to Colorado Mesa University to study theater.

As part of a family tradition, the teen’s mother let each of her five children pick the location of a celebratory senior trip. Chistopher wanted to ride roller coasters, and mother and son discussed a trip to Disneyland or Disney World. After some online research, Christopher chose Six Flags Magic Mountain, known for its thrill rides and DC Comics characters.
“He wanted to see Six Flags,” said Chadwick McGrady, an attorney representing the family in Christopher’s death. “The marketing worked.”

Magic Mountain sits about 35 miles north of downtown Los Angeles, in Valencia, the last notable stop before Interstate 5 climbs a steep stretch known as the Grapevine and drops down into the San Joaquin Valley. The park is aptly named: Roller coasters built into the mountainous terrain hurtle riders down hillsides and through trees, with disorienting turns taken at high velocity.

Christopher rode the X2 on June 2 and again on the morning of June 3. Soon after, reeling from a headache, he texted his mother from a park restroom: “I don’t think I can do any more today. My head is hurting me.”

They went back to the hotel. He had two days to recover before one of the big draws of the trip: DC Heroes and Villains Fest. Christopher “was a huge fan of DC Comics and was looking forward to meeting Batman on Friday, when DC Comics characters would be at the park,” sheriff’s detective Yoon Nam would later write in her report. Friday, June 5, was its opening day, and Christopher was determined not to miss it.

But on the morning of June 4, his head was still hurting him. He had taken refuge in the hotel room’s closet. His mother wasn’t unduly alarmed, because Christopher often retreated to dark spaces at home, a longstanding self-soothing ritual. She listened to the sound of his snoring — until at some point in the afternoon, the sound stopped.
In a statement released through her lawyer, Fascaldo said that her son “had so many dreams, and had his whole life ahead of him.”

After an autopsy, the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner found a large subdural hemorrhage. The cause of death: “blunt force head trauma.” The reason for the injuries was noted as a “history of theme park rides.”
Nam and the medical examiner spoke by phone with Fascaldo, Christopher’s mother, on June 6.

According to a source familiar with the investigation, Fascaldo was composed, recounting a precise chronology of the rides Christopher had ridden. Among them were Full Throttle and the Viper, and, at least twice, the X2.

Nam contacted CalOSHA. She knew that it was responsible for regulating the state’s roller coasters and wanted to make sure the agency was aware that the Magic Mountain rides could have contributed to Christopher’s death.

“I cannot attribute his death to his roller coaster ride experiences with 100% certainty,” Nam wrote in a July 2 email to Bobby Park, who runs the CalOSHA unit regulating roller coasters. “However, at this time, it is possible that he suffered an injury during his visits to the theme park.”
The detective offered to help. “Please let me know if this case warrants additional follow-up by your office,” she wrote. “Feel free to call, text, or email with any questions or concerns.”
In the days after that unanswered email, more parkgoers suffered injuries after riding the X2.
On the evening of July 5, three days after the homicide detective sent her email, Pamela Guillen, 39, rode the coaster with her daughter.

When the car she was riding in trundled back into the station, Guillen’s daughter saw that her mother was “sitting with a vacant stare and her mouth open,” according to a lawsuit the family recently filed. Six Flags has not yet filed a response.

Guillen, who was visiting from Hawaii, managed to stumble off the ride, but a few minutes later park EMTs found her lying unconscious at the exit ramp. Two hours later, Gary Newman, the park’s vice president of maintenance, phoned CalOSHA to report the accident, relaying that a relative had said: “My cousin seemed out of it when she got off the ride so we took her to a bench and she went unconscious.”

The next morning, Scott Prather, a senior safety engineer with CalOSHA’s theme park unit, emailed his boss. According to a state official who has viewed the email, Guillen had been diagnosed with a brain bleed and was going into surgery. The email also said that the ride had been closed for inspection and g-force testing to ensure it was operating as intended.
Six Flags hired a firm that specialized in amusement park rides to conduct the test, according to a CalOSHA source familiar with the investigation.
State officials reviewed the results and authorized Magic Mountain to reopen the ride, the source said.

Then, on July 9, there was another incident, according to CalOSHA records reviewed by ProPublica and L.A. Material. A woman from Nevada was visiting Magic Mountain with her family and others. They were roller coaster enthusiasts and had saved the X2 for their last ride of the day.
As soon as the ride started, the woman sensed something was wrong, according to an email she later sent to CalOSHA’s general inbox.

“The back of my head was repeatedly and forcefully slammed against the back of the seat,” she wrote in the email, which was reviewed by ProPublica and L.A. Material. “I tried holding my head forward and tried pushing it back against the seat to stop the banging, neither worked.”

When the ride stopped, she wasn’t sure whether she could stand. She couldn’t turn her head from side to side. She had nausea, sensitivity to light and a headache that reached “approximately 9 out of 10.”
She wasn’t the only one. “Three of the eight people riding together experienced similar difficulty with their heads repeatedly striking the backs of their seats,” she wrote in August.
She also filed a formal complaint with Six Flags in July but has not received a response, she told ProPublica and L.A. Material.
Two days after the Nevada woman rode the X2, there was another, more serious injury.
Naomi Greer-Wilkinson, a healthy 25-year-old from Los Angeles, rode the X2 on the night of July 11.

According to a lawsuit her family filed in September against the park, Greer-Wilkinson came off the ride “confused and having difficulty walking.” She stumbled off and then lost consciousness. She has since had multiple emergency brain surgeries. The lawsuit says she “remains bedridden, ventilator dependent, unable to speak.” Six Flags has not responded to the lawsuit.
On July 12, the X2 was temporarily shut down. It has not reopened.
In the wake of the ride’s closure, many amusement park patrons are asking how regulators could have missed so many signs of danger.

California law requires CalOSHA to audit records related to every permanent ride each year, including reports of accidents. When amusement park patrons are seriously injured on rides, the theme park must notify regulators immediately.

And yet, again and again, records show, regulators accepted Six Flags’ assertions that the injuries people suffered were not the fault of the X2. ProPublica and L.A. Material reviewed the state’s reports on X2 riders who were taken to the hospital from 2009 to 2022. In more than two-thirds of the cases, or 17 out 23, CalOSHA checked “no” on the form that would determine whether an investigation was warranted.

In September 2022, less than three months after Hawley died, a 28-year-old woman passed out as she exited the ride and hit her head, according to Magic Mountain’s account of the accident in a report filed with the state Paramedics took her to Henry Mayo Newhall Hospital.

Two days after the woman’s injury, Park determined no investigation was necessary. Park wrote: “Patron has pre-existing TBI [traumatic brain injury], diabetes, and has not eaten or consumed anything throughout the day.”
The woman, who survived the incident, sued Six Flags, which denied fault. The case settled in 2025.

The pattern of regulators citing preexisting conditions or rider behavior went back years. In 2011, the state noted that a 21-year-old woman had “a history of panic attacks,” so no investigation of the ride was necessary after she complained of a head injury.

In 2016, a 49-year-old woman hit her head against the headrest and asked for an ambulance. CalOSHA noted that her condition “does not appear to be related to the maintenance or operation of the ride,” adding that she “did not keep her head back” as riders are instructed.

Some of the failures appear related to staffing shortages at CalOSHA. According to a 2025 staffing study by a Sacramento consulting firm commissioned by the state, audits of amusement park rides can be brief. The annual audit for a ride in X2’s class — a review meant to cover accident reports, training and maintenance reports and inspections — lasted an average of 3.7 hours.

The study also found that CalOSHA’s ride unit had been short-staffed for at least three years, with vacancies for its top job and two of four supervisor posts. There were “insufficient” supervisors for “thorough field supervision” and “inspection report review,” the report found.

Documents obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material show Park had voiced frustration about staffing for his division since at least 2019. In an email he sent last week to his supervisor and the state department that oversees CalOSHA, Park wrote: “We have done workload studies, classification studies, begged, pleaded, and warned of the impending doom, and we are still no further along than we were 11 years ago.”
He continued: “We have failed. I have tried to do this, but I cannot continue as the dwindling supply of tools has run out.”
Park had been the CalOSHA official who received the news of Christopher Gibson’s death from Nam, the homicide detective, in early July.
In late August, after the X2 had been closed for more than a month, the detective sent a follow-up email to Park about the teen’s death.
“I never heard back from you regarding my previous email,” Nam wrote. “I saw news about multiple injuries involving the X2 ride at the Six Flags. Is there anything else I need to do?”
Park finally wrote back: “Apologies, I thought we responded.”

Park told the detective that since Christopher had died in a hotel room, there was no way to confirm which roller coasters the teen had ridden and “it would be difficult to determine which ride to assign this to or if it even is associated with a ride.”

Still, a few weeks later, state officials ordered a more sophisticated g-force test of the ride, citing a series of injuries and a death over the summer. CalOSHA said in a statement that there are limits to commonly used ride testing. The standard test focuses on the torso and does not “necessarily establish the full range of movement or physical impacts experienced by an individual rider, including the potential effects on the head and neck,” the agency said. The order for new g-force testing didn’t mention anyone by name, but it did refer to an incident on June 3, the day Christopher left the park with a headache and eventually retreated to his hotel room’s closet, where he died.
The test results are pending.

Later in September, Six Flags announced the ride’s permanent shuttering without acknowledging the injuries or deaths connected with the roller coaster. “While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do,” Magic Mountain president Brian Oerding said in a statement. “Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously.”
The post They Suffered Brain Injuries After Riding a Six Flags Roller Coaster. Regulators Pinned the Blame on Them. appeared first on ProPublica.

articles.title: A Federal Women’s Prison Became a “Rape Club.” After Officials Shut It Down, Rampant Abuse Continued Elsewhere.
articles.author: Keri Blakinger
paras: Officer Felix Wilder sauntered around the women’s prison like he owned the place.

Prone to showing up to work in gold chains and stylish jeans instead of his concrete gray government uniform, the slender 35-year-old moved, one woman said, “like he had just gotten off of a horse from a long ride.” He spoke slowly and eyed the prisoners as they walked through the drab buildings and shadeless yards of the secluded federal lockup in Aliceville, Alabama.

By the fall of 2024, some of the women there had begun to notice him hovering over a soft-spoken immigrant from Mexico who’d been in prison for only a few years. Ela, as she asked to be called, had dark hair, dark eyes and children to get home to back in Utah. Wilder was just a little too close, a little too familiar.
Ela’s cellmate, who asked to be identified as Ana, watched it all with unease. At 40, she knew exactly what that kind of attention from an officer could mean in a women’s prison.

For 15 years, Ana had served her time at Federal Correctional Institution Dublin, a low-security prison in California, where officers had preyed on the women in their care. Sexual misconduct became so rampant that staff and prisoners alike called it a “rape club.” Eventually, the FBI intervened, and prosecutors charged the warden, the chaplain and nine other officers with sexually abusing female prisoners. Hundreds of women — including Ana — came forward to tell what happened to them, not just to investigators, but also to outside lawyers who sued the system to demand change at the Bay Area prison.

Ana had hoped to leave that all behind when she was transferred out of Dublin. But tucked between the pine trees and low-slung churches of rural Alabama, the Aliceville prison had its own brand of menace. The facility had newer buildings but fewer freedoms. The roofs leaked, and sometimes the air smelled faintly of mold. The shorthanded staff often locked the women in their cells for days at a time.
And then there were officers like Wilder, who seemed to be choosing their targets.

Thousands of miles from families they couldn’t call during yet another lockdown, Ana and Ela became allies. They paced. They picked at the lukewarm meals delivered on Styrofoam trays. They stared out the narrow slit of a window.
And then Ela broke down, sobbing as her words tumbled out into the stale prison air.

Two years earlier, an officer had pulled her into a closet and raped her, she told Ana, her voice quavering. Now, she said, it was happening all over again — but this time it was the stylish officer in jeans: Felix Wilder.
Ela said she’d reported the first assault and nothing happened. Now, she didn’t know what to do. If the prison didn’t care about one rape, why would it care about two?

As she listened, Ana felt a dull rage churning in her stomach. She thought of all the things she’d seen and survived at Dublin: the rapes, the harassment, the uncertainty of a life subject to the whims of lascivious men with badges. As she tried to comfort her sobbing cellmate, she wondered whether Aliceville was any better. Maybe, she thought, no place was.

Sitting on her metal bunk, she opened the little address book she’d bought from the prison commissary and flipped to the phone numbers for the lead attorneys in the class action lawsuit against Dublin. “Here,” she told Ela, “you can talk to them.”

The arrests and subsequent convictions of Dublin staff — 10 in all — marked the largest sex abuse scandal in the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ history and a rare moment of accountability in a troubled system where many women had learned to stop expecting it. Suddenly, every branch of government stepped in. A federal judge appointed an outside monitor. A slew of agencies issued reports, and the Justice Department dispatched attorneys to visit and evaluate women’s facilities. Congress passed a law to create a new, independent office to oversee the prison system.

But after the judge made that unprecedented move to appoint outside oversight, in early 2024 the bureau abruptly announced it would shut down Dublin and transfer its more than 600 women — including Ana — to lockups across the country.

Then, quietly, the window of accountability shut. Little appeared to have come of the promised reforms, the site visits and the reports, and Congress never appropriated funding for the new oversight office. More than a dozen current and former federal prison employees told ProPublica and The Marshall Project they’d seen few or no meaningful improvements. One Justice Department official said the only obvious sign of progress was new sexual assault prevention posters.

“Nothing has really changed,” said Alix McLearen, a top Bureau of Prisons official who retired in 2024 after serving as the agency’s first administrator overseeing the women and special populations branch. “We had a horrible crisis, and crisis leads to opportunity, and this is an opportunity that has been completely squandered.”

An official with the federal prison workers union who — like nearly every current employee interviewed for this story — asked not to be named for fear of retaliation, put it even more bluntly: “Nothing has been done to effectively change sexual abuse of inmates within the BOP. Not on a large scale or small scale.”

For the last five years, the culture that spawned a rape club at Dublin has persisted across the system. Reporters at ProPublica and The Marshall Project set out to determine how pervasive the problem of staff sexual abuse inside federal women’s prisons is — and what, if anything, officials have done to solve it. What we found was sexual assault, misconduct or harassment at most of the 27 facilities that currently hold women. We identified more than 185 cases in which prison employees have been accused of sexually abusing people in women’s prisons since 2021, the year the Dublin scandal broke. The cases implicate more than 96 officers at 16 prisons. Of those, just 19 officers have been arrested or convicted.In some cases, officers withheld food or medical care, or threatened to put women in solitary confinement if they refused to comply with sexual demands, court records allege. In others, officers locked them in windowless closets or bathrooms, choked them, or forced them to use sex toys or have sex with each other. In more than a dozen instances, the assaults were so brutal that the women were left bruised and bleeding.

Though some abusers have been prosecuted or removed, insiders say the culture of impunity that allows officers to prey on women remains. Officials have repeatedly refused to acknowledge or failed to act on signs of sexual abuse, we found. More than 25 women said that they were abused by officers who had been reported or investigated before, according to lawsuits we reviewed. In some cases, officers have covered for their abusive colleagues, court records allege. Other times, staff say that they, like the prisoners, have hesitated to report misconduct for fear of retaliation.

At a prison camp in West Virginia, an officer who’d been investigated repeatedly for suspected abuse — but allowed to remain on the job — raped a woman so forcefully that he tore her vaginal lining, according to a lawsuit she filed last year. The officer has been charged with sexually assaulting her and two other women at the camp and has pleaded not guilty. His case is set for trial early next year.

At Federal Medical Center Carswell, a facility in North Texas, an officer allegedly forced two women to have a threesome with him in his office, where he’d rigged up a doorbell to alert him if anyone came by, court filings show. A civil lawsuit has been stayed pending a criminal investigation.
“We had a horrible crisis, and crisis leads to opportunity, and this is an opportunity that has been completely squandered.”Alix McLearen, former Bureau of Prisons official

And at Aliceville, Wilder, the officer who allegedly assaulted Ela, also abused at least 17 other women, many of whom were facing deportation after they finished serving their sentences, according to court records and interviews. He allegedly didn’t stop until the FBI showed up at the facility in the fall of 2024, and federal prosecutors eventually charged him with sexually abusing seven women. He has pleaded not guilty and is awaiting trial.

“I’m pretty sure everybody knew what was going on and they just didn’t care,” one of the women told ProPublica and The Marshall Project in a phone interview from the federal prison in Fort Worth, Texas.

We found that abuse continued even as the facilities kept passing federally mandated sexual assault prevention audits. The Texas medical facility had a flawless audit the same year the FBI arrived to investigate a paramedic whom at least 18 women have accused of sexual assault, records show. Likewise, Aliceville got perfect marks during the same time period that Wilder was allegedly preying on Ela and other women.

The officers union called sexual abuse “completely unacceptable” and blamed persistent staffing shortages for helping to create an environment that allows it to go undetected. “If we are serious about protecting inmates and maintaining safe, secure federal prisons, we have to address the staffing crisis head-on,” the union said in a statement, noting that more watchful eyes would mean “fewer opportunities for inappropriate conduct to occur behind closed doors.”
Bureau of Prisons spokesperson Randilee Giamusso said the federal prison system has “zero tolerance” for sexual abuse and harassment. “We take all allegations of sexual abuse seriously,” she said.

Giamusso highlighted the bureau’s recently revamped policy on sexually abusive behavior, which is intended to ensure that allegations are more thoroughly investigated. It also eliminates any mention of transgender or intersex people, whom federal law identifies as particularly vulnerable to sexual abuse in prison. She did not provide further details or address any specific cases, saying the bureau does not comment on pending litigation. Officers mentioned in this story, as well as representatives for the prisons, either did not respond or declined to comment on specific allegations.

As Ana and the other Dublin women, now scattered to other facilities, realized that no one was going to stop the abuse, they began to take matters into their own hands. Across the country, they encouraged other women to speak out about what had happened to them — and told them what they could do about it.

The volume of abuse allegations ballooned so rapidly that the legal team handling the Dublin case had to refer scores of potential clients to other lawyers, some of whom have taken on so many federal prison sex abuse cases that it’s become the primary focus of their law practice. We continued receiving new lawsuits, tort claims and allegations of abuse up until publication of this story.

“There has been so much reporting on Dublin as an aberration,” said Susan Beaty, one of the lawyers spearheading the class action suit. “But I think it’s actually incredibly representative. I think it’s happening at basically every BOP women’s prison.”

As she comforted her cellmate at Aliceville, Ana thought back to her first months at Dublin — before she’d learned how to recognize abuse in prison and before she’d seen just how much of it there was.
Back then, around 2010, it seemed that almost every day she saw a handful of women eating Mexican takeout for lunch — hot meals too mouth-watering to have come from the spartan prison kitchen.

At the time, Ana was just 25 and at the beginning of a lengthy sentence stemming from her involvement in her husband’s drug-trafficking operation. So while she suspected the smuggled-in meals were the sign of some nefarious quid pro quo arrangement with the officers, she didn’t ask questions, partly because she was afraid and partly because the women shared their coveted contraband meals. “So I would just eat it and shut up,” she said.

Under federal law, all sexual contact between prison staff and people in custody is a felony — and for good reason. Prisoners cannot meaningfully give consent when they’re propositioned by people who control every aspect of their lives, from when they get fed to whether they face disciplinary sanctions that could land them in solitary confinement. So although prison sex abuse sometimes involves violent rape, it often relies on subtle coercion and grooming.

Poor conditions and scarcity behind bars turn basic necessities into valuable commodities that officers can leverage to create the illusion of a “relationship” — one built on exchanging sexual favors for extra privileges and little gifts, like contraband makeup, extra tampons or a few more minutes at visitation.

As one high-ranking prison official explained: “The women are getting small trinkets. It’s not big things that we can trace. He’s bringing in a hamburger, a Subway sandwich. It’s heartbreaking to look at the value of the things that are being passed.”

Many times, those seeming relationships turn volatile — and violent. In Ana’s case, it began when one Dublin officer started being unusually nice to her, according to her lawsuit. He’d rush across the unit to unlock doors for her or call her into his office to talk alone. Ana thought they’d developed a rapport. But over time, he groomed her with personal questions and meager privileges. Once, he told her he’d had a sexual dream about her. Then, according to her lawsuit, he kissed her and eventually raped her.

Telling prison investigators didn’t seem like an option; Ana had already learned the hard way about the risks of reporting errant staff. A few years earlier, she had helped another prisoner file a complaint about staff misconduct. Afterward, she said, both women were sent to solitary confinement. For two weeks, Ana spent 23 hours a day locked in a cell barely bigger than an elevator. She got cold food, had no access to the phone and was barred from seeing visitors.

Prison officials often isolate those who report abuse, ostensibly for their own protection, even though the Justice Department has found this practice has a “chilling effect” that discourages people from reporting abuse. A federal prison spokesperson said the agency’s policy does not require that people who report abuse be put in solitary — but that sometimes it is the only adequate option.

It’s not just prisoners who are afraid to report wrongdoing. Although staff are required to report misconduct under bureau policy, in lawsuits and interviews, officers say they, too, worry about retaliation.

“You see all the sexual abuse, how they treat inmates. If you bring that to their attention, it’s like you’re doing the wrong thing,” said a former correctional officer at the prison camp for women in Bryan, Texas. In 2024, she reported several co-workers for having sexual contact with incarcerated women. She resigned last year after the warden moved to fire her for unprofessional conduct, documents show.

Even when witnesses or victims do report abuse, investigators rarely conclude that it occurred. As of 2022, less than 10% of allegations against Bureau of Prisons employees were substantiated, meaning investigators found it more likely than not that the abuse happened in those cases. In some instances, investigators decided there was evidence the abuse didn’t occur. But more than 75% of the time, they said there wasn’t enough evidence to make a determination either way.

Officers accused of abuse face an internal disciplinary process that can take years. In many cases, they can simply retire or resign, knowing that the agency will no longer have jurisdiction to punish them once they leave. They could still face criminal charges — but bureau insiders say that many cases don’t reach that point because investigators abandon the criminal probes when an officer resigns. “Staff would know that if they were having sex with inmates, the worst that would happen is that you would have to find a new job,” one former prison official said.

The landmark law intended to combat sex abuse, the 2003 Prison Rape Elimination Act — widely known as PREA — mandates employee training and regular audits but lacks a serious enforcement mechanism. Auditors are primarily looking for policy compliance, not signs of abuse. “A facility may have widespread sexual abuse, but they’re still meeting compliance on the things they’re required to do,” said Kendra Prisk, a PREA auditor who has evaluated several federal prisons, including Aliceville.
Do You Have a Story to Share About This Topic?
Beth Schwartzapfel and I are continuing to report on this issue and want to hear from any prisoners or prison staff who have been sexually harassed or abused in the Federal Bureau of Prisons.

I welcome any tips leading to tough accountability stories about the legal system. Right now, I’m particularly interested in hearing from federal prison employees and federal prisoners with information about untold and revelatory stories.

At Dublin, Ana said she watched the officer who’d been bringing in burritos get walked off the job by investigators. He was, according to an Associated Press investigation and several agency sources, one of about a dozen Dublin workers in the early 2010s who were quietly removed from their posts — but not prosecuted — over sex abuse allegations.

In September 2021, a new round of problems at Dublin burst into public view when the FBI arrested the facility’s warden, Ray Garcia. He was eventually charged with sexually abusing multiple women all over the compound — then lying to cover it up. In one instance, prosecutors say he abused a woman while PREA auditors were visiting. Though Garcia was later convicted and sentenced to nearly six years in prison, his attorney, Kevin Little, told ProPublica and The Marshall Project that Garcia maintained that he is not guilty.

The arrest of such a high-ranking official sent shockwaves through the system. Members of Congress began asking questions. The head of the agency, Michael Carvajal, announced that he would step down, a move he said in a recent interview was driven by concerns that Congress would not support the bureau until he left. Ultimately, 10 Dublin officers pleaded guilty or were convicted at trial, and one walked free after two hung juries.

While several of the Dublin officers could not be reached or did not respond to requests for comment, one did. John Bellhouse, who was a safety supervisor, emailed ProPublica and The Marshall Project from a federal prison in Louisiana, where he is serving a 63-month sentence after he was convicted of sexually abusing two women. Bellhouse insisted he is innocent and said the problem at Dublin was that the lower-ranking staff were “too comfortable” at the facility and too familiar with the prisoners. “It was very junior high school,” he wrote.
To Ana and the other women at Dublin, the rash of charges had made it seem for a moment like there might be change. But it soon became clear the problems were far more entrenched.
“BOP Was Putting on a Show”
In the wake of the indictments at Dublin, prison officials were dispatched across the country beginning in 2022 to inspect other women’s prisons and generate internal reports.

That spring, at the low-security prison in Tallahassee, Florida, most of the women surveyed for the “Women’s Institution Cultural Assessment” said they were afraid of reprisals if they spoke freely, according to a copy reviewed by ProPublica and The Marshall Project. The last time officials visited, they said, officers had punished the women with “shakedowns” — in which officers ransack cells and destroy belongings — and told them it was in retaliation for talking to the visitors. Despite noting this and “several concerning observations,” the bureau found that sexual safety was “not determined to be a problem” at the facility.

Since then, at least 10 prisoners have filed legal claims saying they were abused by Tallahassee officers in the same year as the assessment. Six said they were sexually assaulted by a single officer, Lenton Hatten, who had previously been reprimanded by prison officials at another facility for putting money in women’s commissary accounts, “which was a warning sign of inappropriate relations,” according to multiple lawsuits. He was ultimately sentenced to three months in prison for repeatedly abusing one woman after DNA tied him to the crime. In legal filings, attorneys for the prison system admitted that Hatten sexually abused that woman but denied that he assaulted any of the others. They also denied that officials had failed to train or supervise Hatten properly. Neither Hatten nor his attorney responded to requests for comment.

At Carswell, in the summer of 2022, multiple prisoners told officials that prison staff had held town hall meetings before the site visit, threatening repercussions if anyone reported their concerns, the assessment found. Nonetheless, the team concluded that women at Carswell overwhelmingly felt it was a “physically and sexually safe environment.”

But that year, at least seven women were sexually abused by four different Carswell employees, according to allegations in civil lawsuits they’ve since filed. In one case, a woman who was partially paralyzed and required a wheelchair said she was violently sodomized in the shower by an officer who attended her Bible study group. When he heard people coming, she said he dropped her on the floor, leaving her alone to crawl back to her wheelchair, crying and bloodied. Months later, when she finally reported the assault, the nurse on duty told her she’d reported that same officer for sexually harassing other prisoners and nothing had been done about it, according to her lawsuit.

All the suits are still pending. Among the staffers named in them, only Hatten has been prosecuted. In many cases, it’s not clear whether any of the employees were disciplined by the Bureau of Prisons. The prisons agency would not answer questions about the assessments’ findings, though a spokesperson said it has continued to visit prisons and conduct assessments, which it does not release to the public.

Later in 2022, a highly publicized Senate subcommittee investigation found the problem of prison sexual assault was more widespread than previously understood and, around the same time, the Justice Department’s inspector general issued a report criticizing the bureau’s handling of staff misconduct investigations.

Meanwhile, the Bureau of Prisons’ parent agency, the Justice Department, put together a working group that recommended prison officials “enhance prevention of sexual misconduct” by promoting “stronger leadership” at women’s facilities, improving staff training and installing more cameras.

In mid-2023, the department began dispatching its own teams to survey women’s prisons and make sure they were carrying out the working group’s recommendations. Nikhil Ramnaney, a former Justice Department attorney who participated in a visit to the SeaTac lockup in Washington state that summer, said the department notified prison officials in advance, giving them time to prepare. “BOP was putting on a show,” he said. And when Ramnaney and the other visitors interviewed women, the facility’s top officials stood nearby. When asked if they felt safe reporting abuse, the women offered “positive and lukewarm answers,” Ramnaney said. “In hindsight, what else were they going to say?”

Another Department of Justice attorney who visited Carswell offered a similar assessment, and both said the department never released findings from those site visits. Neither could identify any meaningful changes the agency made.

Since then, officials from the Bureau of Prisons and the Justice Department have repeatedly said the agency is working to implement the working group’s recommendations. But when asked a series of detailed questions about the status of specific recommendations, the Justice Department deferred to the prison agency. Giamusso, the prisons spokesperson, said in an email that information was “not readily available.” She added, “We have more work to do, and we are committed to doing that work.”

By the end of 2023, there were growing signs that women were being abused at other facilities. At the camp in Bryan, Texas, it was an open secret that officers were groping women and pressuring them into unwanted sex acts, according to women and staff previously interviewed by The Marshall Project and NBC News. At the federal jail in Chicago, an officer groped and sexually assaulted at least four women in December alone, according to an indictment. That officer pleaded not guilty, and the case is ongoing.

And perhaps most disturbingly, the abuse continued at Dublin, even while the prison was under the scrutiny of the courts and Congress in the wake of Warden Garcia’s arrest. In addition to the hundreds who said they were abused before 2021, at least 47 prisoners alleged abuse by staffers after that. Many of those allegations have not been previously reported, and many of the alleged abusers have not been prosecuted.

The abuse continued even after the agency replaced Garcia. And it continued after a sprawling legal team — including attorneys from the advocacy organization Rights Behind Bars, the law firm Rosen Bien Galvan & Grunfeld and the nonprofit legal group California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice — filed the class action lawsuit against the bureau in the summer of 2023 on behalf of Ana and hundreds of other Dublin women. They alleged the Bureau of Prisons’ systems for preventing and responding to sexual abuse were so inadequate that everyone at Dublin was at risk. The following year, the government claimed in court filings that sexual abuse was by then “virtually non-existent” at Dublin and that the facility was “not currently a sexualized environment.”

A few weeks before that claim, a Dublin officer had allegedly slammed Antonina Troyer against the wall of her cell and raped her, according to a lawsuit she filed later, which has since been stayed. Troyer said three years after she reported him, she received a letter stating that her allegation was not sustained but offering no further information. The officer, who did not respond to requests for comment, was not prosecuted and still worked for the agency as of November.
“You have a huge system that just steamrolls everybody, and you’re already considered to be not trustworthy,” Troyer said in an interview. “Our word means practically nothing.”

By March 2024, the federal judge overseeing the Dublin lawsuit had grown noticeably frustrated with what she called the prison agency’s sluggish response. Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers issued a scathing order and appointed a so-called “special master” to oversee promised reforms.

Days later, the bureau abruptly announced that it would shut down Dublin — then asked the judge to dismiss the case. The judge demurred, saying the idea that closure solved the agency’s problems “strains credulity.”

Ana and the other women at Dublin were shackled and taken to other facilities around the country in what seemed like an unusually torturous process. In letters and interviews, women recounted how some officers screamed at them, threatened to shoot them or left them without water for hours. “With their behavior and the noise of the cocked guns,” one woman wrote, “I was sure they were going to kill us.” An internal affairs investigation later determined that all the transport officers had acted “within policy” even though, in some cases, other prison staff corroborated the women’s accounts.
“It Felt Just Like Another Dublin”

For Beaty and the other San Francisco-based attorneys heading up the legal team for the class action lawsuit, building a case against the federal government now became much more complicated. To interview dozens more survivors, they had to travel across the country to remote prisons.

That October, Beaty and fellow attorney Kara Janssen paid their first visit to Aliceville. They’d just come from a legal conference in Atlanta, where they’d given a presentation on their work at Dublin, then rented cars to drive four hours to a hotel in Tuscaloosa. After another hour on the road — once they’d nearly reached the Mississippi border — the bleak, boxy buildings of a federal prison rose up out of the endless forest.

When the lawyers walked through the front door, the prison staff seemed so unaccustomed to legal visitors that they weren’t sure how to sign them in. “It felt like nobody had come there in a long time,” said Janssen.

Over the next three days, she and Beaty took down statements from more than 70 women, most transfers from Dublin. Some described the rough move or their trouble getting basic medical care. But others told new stories of abuse, this time at Aliceville. The medical staff who forced them to dance. The officers who assaulted them in closets, and the other staff who pretended not to see.

One of the women who talked to them was Ela. She’d landed behind bars five years earlier, after FBI agents arrested her in a meth bust. It was the first time she’d been in real trouble. She was sentenced to seven years in federal prison and eventually ended up in Aliceville, where, in early 2022, an officer pulled her into a closet and pushed her to her knees, forcing her to perform oral sex on him before vaginally raping her, according to a tort claim filed on her behalf. When she reported the incident to prison officials, she said they yelled at her and fired her from her job in the prison’s safety department. Traumatized and distraught, she began cutting herself. Eventually, she asked to see a psychiatrist but left feeling worse after the psychiatrist made fun of her, according to the narrative laid out in her legal claim.

About a year later, Wilder — the officer in stylish jeans — started circling, according to the claim. He was flirtatious at first, talking about his own romantic encounters and asking about her family back home. Then, one day in the spring of 2023, she said he forced her into a utility closet and made her perform oral sex on him. A few months later, he locked her in that same closet for two hours, returning three times to rape her, according to the legal claim.

Ela wasn’t the only woman Wilder allegedly targeted. Other women had reported him for similar behavior, but his abuse continued until the fall of 2024, according to court filings and interviews. That September, investigators questioned Ela about her earlier abuser, who had by then pleaded guilty to assaulting two other women. But even though Ela had already confided in Ana about Wilder, she was reluctant to tell prison officials. “I was very scared to speak out,” she said in emails in Spanish to ProPublica and The Marshall Project.

Investigators paid another visit days later — and that time she told them everything. “I would not want the chain of victims to continue,” she said. “We had to put a stop to it.” Wilder was walked off the prison property that day. But officers threw Ela into solitary confinement for nearly two weeks. They told her it was for her safety — “which really wasn’t safe at all because it was a nightmare,” she said.

“You have a huge system that just steamrolls everybody, and you’re already considered to be not trustworthy. Our word means practically nothing.”Antonina Troyer, formerly incarcerated at Federal Correctional Institution Dublin

And while Wilder was eventually indicted for sexually abusing seven women, 11 others — including Ela — have also accused him of sexual assault in civil claims, including two lawsuits. In both of those cases, a court has paused the proceedings until the criminal charges against him are resolved. Apart from his not guilty plea, Wilder has not responded in court or to repeated requests for comment.
By the time Beaty and Janssen arrived at Aliceville, the women were skittish, rattled by the abuse, the retaliation, the prodding FBI agents.
“A lot of people were really scared,” Janssen said. “It felt just like another Dublin.” As she got in the car to leave, Janssen broke down crying.

In the months following the Aliceville trip, the lawyers traveled to prisons in California, Connecticut, Texas, Florida and Wisconsin to speak to Dublin victims. At almost every stop, women told them of abuse happening in that institution, too.

In early 2025, over the new Trump administration’s objections, Gonzalez Rogers, the judge in the Dublin class action suit, approved a sweeping consent decree — a first for the federal prison system. It included pathways to early release, increased protections against retaliation and two more years of court-mandated oversight for the Dublin survivors.

It would not be enough to protect those who were still incarcerated. Even as their lawyers prepared civil suits, Ana and the other Dublin women became targets for harassment at their new prisons. At some facilities, staff derisively referred to them as “Dublin girls” or “Dublin bitches” and refused to give them prison jobs, according to interviews and court papers. Elsewhere, other prisoners viewed them as snitches and held their decision to come forward against them.

The women also continued to face sexual abuse. After getting shipped out of Dublin, the survivors reported almost 40 instances of abuse at their new prisons during the first six months of the court-appointed monitoring, according to monthly reports filed in federal court.

Abuse allegations continue to extend far beyond Dublin survivors. In interviews and legal filings, ProPublica and The Marshall Project uncovered accusations of sexual abuse at a prison camp in California, a low-security prison in Wisconsin and a notoriously troubled facility in West Virginia.
And earlier this year, the FBI showed up at Carswell, a facility so troubled that one woman described it in court filings as “a federal prison that became a hunting ground.”

Investigators uncovered a cluster of allegations against paramedic Preston Emert, who was removed from his job after 18 women accused him of sexually abusive behavior, according to court filings and internal bureau correspondence. Emert targeted women with addiction issues and medical problems, demanding sex in exchange for drugs and medical treatments, according to several women, their attorneys and a top bureau official.

“I have seizures and would need help and in order to get it I would have to have sex with him,” Olivia Floyd said in a letter to reporters. Emert is one of 12 Carswell employees accused of sexual assault in the last five years. He has not been charged, and bureau officials said in November he is still employed as a paramedic at Carswell.

Last month, his boss — the health services supervisor who records show fielded at least one of the early complaints about the paramedic’s behavior — was arrested after he admitted to investigators that he was having sex with a woman incarcerated there. He has not yet entered a plea.
“No Substantive Long-Term Changes”

Despite evidence of persistent abuse throughout the system, the Bureau of Prisons now appears poised to have less oversight than ever. The landmark consent decree is set to expire early next year. The Office of Inspector General, the Justice Department’s watchdog that has the power to investigate and recommend reforms, has suffered staffing shortages in recent years as the Trump administration has pushed to slash its budget. Meanwhile, hoping to shore up its staffing levels, the bureau recently announced it would allow new officers to start with fewer qualifications and lower pay.

“It’s almost as if they’ve learned nothing,” said Shanna Rifkin, general counsel for FAMM, a nonpartisan organization that advocates for criminal justice reform. “They need staff who are well-trained and well-compensated, and to lower the qualifications when you already have rampant sex abuse and drugs being brought in — what do they think is going to happen?”

Two years after Congress passed the Federal Prison Oversight Act, the ombuds office it mandated still does not exist. The Trump Department of Justice has failed to release a projected budget and progress report, even after both chambers of Congress directed it to do so by April of this year. And lawmakers have yet to appropriate any money for it.

Within the Bureau of Prisons, the effects of the intended reforms have been minimal. The agency has installed more cameras and restructured its Office of Internal Affairs, though under the new structure, staff at individual prisons typically still investigate their coworkers. “I think small things were changed — like the signage about how to report [abuse] needed fixing,” said former Justice Department attorney Marnie Shiels. “There were no substantive long-term changes from this that I know of.”

Lawyers say it’s also becoming harder for civil cases to succeed. So far, the federal government has agreed to pay $116 million to settle lawsuits with the first 103 victims of Dublin. Roughly 300 more cases are working their way through the legal system, including the one brought by Ana, who has since been released from prison. The man who abused her was never criminally charged, and he died while under investigation.

Trump’s Justice Department has offered paltry payouts in some cases and reneged on signed agreements that could have avoided protracted litigation in others, according to sources familiar with the situation. Lauren Bis, a spokesperson for the White House, referred questions to federal prison officials.

Legal experts also point to a recent, troubling precedent. In 2024, a federal judge in Alabama threw out a lawsuit brought by a woman at Aliceville who had been raped by an officer. The judge, Scott Coogler, sided with the Justice Department in ruling that the prison system wasn’t liable because the officer “was acting outside the scope of his employment” when he sexually assaulted her while on duty. The decision is pending appeal.

“This case could make it incredibly hard for anyone abused in government custody to seek accountability from the BOP,” said Deborah Golden, who is representing dozens of women in cases about their sexual abuse at federal prisons. “I hope that doesn’t happen.”

To the lawyers at the forefront of this fight, the fallout from Dublin has come to a disappointing conclusion. “It should not be hard to go to work and not force someone to give you a blow job,” Janssen said. “That is an extremely easy rule to follow. And I can only think that it’s just a complete lack of accountability.”

As for the Bureau of Prisons, it’s already returning to a familiar playbook. Earlier this year, the bureau announced plans to stop housing women at Aliceville and turn the facility into a men’s prison. Ela has since been released. But the rest of the women will, once again, be scattered across the country.
How We Counted Abuse Cases

Reporters searched federal court records and civil lawsuits and interviewed currently and formerly incarcerated survivors of sexual abuse, prison officials, and civil rights attorneys to compile a list of allegations that met the criteria for “sexual abuse” under the Prison Rape Elimination Act. They included only abuse allegedly committed by a BOP staffer against prisoners at women’s facilities operated by the Bureau of Prisons. There were 172 cases involving women and 15 in which the victims were transgender men. Allegations were sourced from an official record — including tort claims, lawsuits, criminal filings and internal agency documents — or the individual themselves, in which cases reporters corroborated their accounts with contemporaneous witness statements, journal entries, or letters; court filings; sworn statements; and other documentation.
The post A Federal Women’s Prison Became a “Rape Club.” After Officials Shut It Down, Rampant Abuse Continued Elsewhere. appeared first on ProPublica.

articles.title: Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands
articles.author: Mark Olalde
paras: A dozen Democrats in Congress are calling for limiting or banning the construction of data centers on public lands. The moves follow reporting from ProPublica that revealed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the White House’s artificial intelligence push, has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies.

“Our public lands aren’t a piggy bank for Trump’s powerful friends,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said in a social media post that pointed to ProPublica’s reporting. Her office told the news organization that the senator, who serves on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is working on legislation to regulate data centers on public lands and will use the panel’s oversight authority to address concerns about transparency surrounding them.

Burgum was asked about ProPublica’s reporting at a recent event hosted by the conservative website Daily Caller. He said that his financial reporting and ethics were “clean as a whistle,” and that he invested in software companies before they turned to AI. “I don’t even know all the names of the companies that are in the portfolio,” he said of his vast wealth.

ProPublica found that hundreds of President Donald Trump’s political appointees in the executive branch, or their spouses, held stocks, owned equity or had other financial ties to AI companies and data center developers. Other offices, including the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, defended their political leadership, saying the appointees followed lawyers’ guidance and had not violated ethics rules.

Our reporting also found that a U.S. Geological Survey study released earlier this year identified an area of U.S. Department of the Interior land nearly the size of Montana that might be suitable for data centers.
Several members of Congress pledged to float legislation to ban data center development on this land.

“These lands are treasured and must be protected for future generations to benefit from and enjoy,” Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said in a statement. In mid-November, she filed the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, which would ban data center construction on land managed by the Interior Department and the Forest Service.

Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan in July filed the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act, which would also prohibit their build-out on federally managed land. The measure was dead on arrival in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives.

“I’m going to continue building the coalition for our bill, and at the same time, I’m going to push the Oversight Committee to investigate the outrageous corruption of the Trump Administration,” she told ProPublica in a statement.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the pushback from Democrats in Congress.

Also speaking up were Rep. Jared Huffman of California and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members of the natural resources committees in their respective chambers. Huffman and Heinrich are in line to take up the gavel in those committees in January when Democrats retake the majority.
“These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Public lands belong in public hands.”

Heinrich is pushing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a generational overhaul of the legislation governing how federal agencies permit major developments. Republicans in Congress and the White House support the swift passage of the bill, as do some Democrats. The more environmentally minded members of the Democratic caucus, however, are calling on Heinrich to slow down and force a better deal once Congress reconvenes next year with Democratic majorities.

Environmental policy experts agree that permitting reform is desperately needed to address climate change by allowing the faster build-out of renewable electricity generation and transmission lines. But green groups including the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council and League of Conservation Voters oppose the bill because it would likely also lead to more fossil fuel projects while limiting input on projects from Native American tribes.

The legislation presents a mixed bag for data centers. A spokesperson for Heinrich defended the permitting reform bill, pointing out that it would require data center companies to bear their own costs for connecting to and upgrading the electrical grid. But the legislation would also streamline approval of natural gas-fired power plants, which power many data centers. The bill would make it more difficult to take away a permit after it’s issued.

Meanwhile, the Interior Department released a five-year strategic plan last week that includes a proposal to sell off public lands or pursue “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges and direct transfer of lands.” It is unclear whether the department intends to offer to sell to companies or only to local, state and tribal governments. Researchers who study natural resources policy told ProPublica that the country’s foundational land management law lays out steps that must be followed to dispose of federal land, steps that will be difficult for the Trump administration to legally navigate.

Still, with permits for data centers pending before the Interior Department, the release of the strategic plan sparked fear that developers might try to buy federal land. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for conservation group Save Our Parks, said the plan was another attempt by Burgum to “sell off what’s left to AI data center developers and his extractive resource buddies.”
The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment on its proposal to sell federal land.
The post Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands appeared first on ProPublica.

articles.title: I Photographed Her Parents as They Were Sentenced for Her Twin’s Death. Years Later, I Photographed Her Life.
articles.author: Beth Nakamura
paras: About eight years ago, I was assigned to photograph the sentencing of Travis and Sarah Mitchell, a couple with deep roots in an insular faith-healing sect outside of Portland, Oregon.

The Mitchells, as members of the Followers of Christ, adhere to a doctrine that forbids medical care. Instead, followers rely on healing through faith. So when Sarah Mitchell gave birth prematurely to twins in 2017 — and both gasped for breath in their first hours — the couple didn’t rush them to an emergency room. Instead, they turned to prayer.

One twin, Ginnifer, lived for four hours, each one a struggle. The family eventually sought medical care for her surviving twin sister, Evelyn, but only after the county’s deputy medical examiner arrived at the location of the home birth and learned, though not right away, of Evelyn’s existence. Even then, he had to seek help from police, who arrived at the Oregon City home and told reluctant family members to take the struggling infant to the hospital or they’d do it themselves.

The Mitchells pleaded guilty to criminally negligent homicide in the death of their infant daughter, Ginnifer, and to criminal mistreatment for failing to seek medical care for her surviving twin, Evelyn. The couple’s lawyer told the judge that the Mitchells grieved the loss of Ginnifer and loved Evelyn. “Travis and Sarah are utterly sincere, decent and caring human beings,” he told the judge. (The Mitchells and their lawyer did not respond to ProPublica and The Oregonian’s recent requests to be interviewed.)

Today, my memory of the sentencing is more montage than detail. But I remember the crowded gallery, the couple in black-and-white-striped prison clothing, and their prison sentence of more than six years. Evelyn, who within days of her birth had been placed in the custody of Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, another couple in the Followers of Christ, wasn’t present. She remained in the couple’s permanent care.
The Mitchells went off to prison, and I went on with my life.

Such is the grinding rhythm of the daily news cycle. So often I see people on their worst day — and then never again. Stories don’t really end, of course, but my role as a photojournalist is limited. I’m an observer rather than a participant, seeing mostly slivers of the human experience that offer only a window into the whole. It’s rare that I get to see what happens next.

Never would I have dreamed that the surviving baby in this case, Evelyn, would be someone I’d later come to know and care about through my work. But that’s precisely what happened eight years after that courtroom scene played out, when I began documenting the lives of Evelyn and her parents, the Phillipses. (In a legal filing in an ongoing case relating to Evelyn’s custody, the Mitchells criticized the Phillipses for allowing her to participate in our coverage.) The resulting story, a collaboration between ProPublica and The Oregonian, is one of several recently published about faith healing and the Followers of Christ church. It intimately explores the Phillipses’ journey out of the sect and illustrates how changes in Oregon state law — in contrast to neighboring Idaho, where the Followers have a handful of churches — have led to a reduction in child deaths.

To spend time around 9-year-old Evelyn is to behold a luminous, magnetic force of nature. It’s impossible to imagine this same girl as a premature baby so small that the only items that fit her were doll clothes purchased from the supermarket toy aisle.

For months, as I documented Evelyn’s life — from her baptism to her home life to doctors’ appointments — my journalism colleagues worked on their own pieces of our project. Teresa Mahoney, video editor at The Oregonian, produced a video introduction to the story that included a sequence of footage recorded by body cameras worn by police officers who stood outside Evelyn’s grandparents’ house that night, at first nudging, then ordering, Evelyn’s family to get her to the hospital. Each time I viewed it, as I watched the officers politely letting time slip away, I’d need to regulate my own breathing as I imagined Evelyn on the other side of that door, struggling to breathe herself.

I hope that reporter Noelle Crombie’s words, Teresa’s video and my photographs allow readers to see not only the journey of the couple who are raising Evelyn as their own but also the surviving — indeed, thriving — twin I came to know. That Evelyn is alive at all is, depending on your worldview, a miracle.
My work is all about observing and capturing moments, about freezing time. Here, I was witnessing the unfolding of time. I got to see what happened next.
The post I Photographed Her Parents as They Were Sentenced for Her Twin’s Death. Years Later, I Photographed Her Life. appeared first on ProPublica.

articles.title: Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers
articles.author: Robert Faturechi
paras: When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world’s largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers.
The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports.

Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients:

The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies.
Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist.
Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses.

The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for, and it has denied ProPublica’s requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.

Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, “returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing,” though they generally don’t say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups.

But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers.

“Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn’t anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund,” said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. “It really explains why it’s so important for the government, when they’re doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don’t pay extra money and not get it back.”

The chain reaction that led to these bonuses began in the first months of Trump’s second term. In February 2025, Trump declared a national emergency over illegal drugs coming in across the border and unilaterally announced new tariffs on goods from the countries he deemed responsible: Canada, Mexico and China.

Then, in April, he declared a second national emergency, this one over the U.S. trade deficit — the fact that the U.S. was importing more than it exported. Declaring it “Liberation Day,” Trump unveiled a poster in the Rose Garden detailing his most sweeping tariffs yet on goods from more than 100 countries.
“Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money.”Gregory Germain, corporate law professor at Syracuse University
Those tariffs remained in place, with some tweaks, until earlier this year when the Supreme Court struck them down, ruling that Trump had needed congressional approval to impose them.

That left the federal government scrambling to figure out how to refund billions in duties it had collected over the prior year on more than 53 million imported shipments. U.S. Customs and Border Protection set up an online application system. But only the direct payers of the tariffs — called the “importers of record” — are eligible to apply, not the businesses and consumers who took a hit downstream.

The New York Federal Reserve Bank, which analyzed the prices of a broad swath of goods, found that 26% of the tariff costs were eaten by American customers; a study from Harvard Business School put the estimate at 43%. One study estimated that Trump’s tariffs cost typical American households about $1,000 last year.

The administration and Congress have not placed constraints on how companies use the tariff refunds, though there have been calls to do so. After the Supreme Court ruling, a group of Democratic senators wrote to the president, asking if he would require companies to pass along part of their payments to consumers and assign penalties to those that did not. Doing otherwise, said Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker and Peter Welch, would render the refunds “a giveaway to giant corporations that amounts to theft from the middle class.”

Though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has denied that the tariffs resulted in significantly higher prices, he has acknowledged the fundamental unfairness of only importers of record getting the refund. “I got a feeling the American people won’t see it,” he said in February at an Economic Club of Dallas event.

Bessent has made the argument that it’s the Democrats who challenged the tariffs in court, not the administration that imposed the tariffs, who are responsible for the transfer of wealth from American consumers to companies.

“The Democratic attorney generals who filed a ridiculous lawsuit against this administration wanted the money to go back to the payer of record,” he said at a press conference. “If I hear another Democratic legislator make the inane remark, ‘The American people should get the money’ — the American people had the money in the U.S. Treasury and we were forced to give it back.”
“I got a feeling the American people won’t see” the refund money.Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent

In some cases, companies have said that they will be splitting at least some of their refund checks with their customers. ProPublica’s analysis shows these companies’ customers are generally other businesses, not average consumers. Among them is Varex Imaging Corp. in Utah, which sells X-ray imaging components for medical businesses and cargo screeners. Varex and firms like it have not elaborated on why they are passing along refunds, but trade experts suspect these business-to-business vendors have detailed contracts that itemize tariff costs.

Shipping companies, like UPS and FedEx, have set up online portals for customers seeking refunds. Though the firms are technically importers of record, they imported goods on behalf of businesses and individuals that paid them to ship products. The companies are itemizing how much customers paid in tariffs and reimbursing them.

A series of lawsuits are attempting to force companies that sell directly to consumers to share some of their refunds. Dozens of firms have been sued, including big-box stores Walmart and Target and apparel companies such as Nike and Lululemon. Apparel and leather costs were some of the hardest hit by Trump’s tariffs. Legal analysts have cast doubt on whether these lawsuits will succeed, though some trade experts have speculated that businesses that used the tariffs as cover to raise prices more than they needed to might settle to avoid embarrassing disclosures.

One of the companies facing a lawsuit is Stanley Black & Decker, the toolmaker that ProPublica found was using some of its refund on bonuses. The named plaintiff is a Wisconsin resident who bought a handheld blower, an impact wrench, a hedge trimmer and other tools from the company last year, but the lawsuit seeks to represent thousands of other customers as well.

“Unless restrained by this Court,” the complaint reads, the company “stands to recover the same tariff payments twice — once from consumers through tariff-inflated prices and again from the federal government through tariff refunds.”
On multiple occasions, the company has acknowledged publicly that it was raising prices because of the tariffs.

The month before the November 2024 election, as Trump was campaigning on dramatic new tariffs, the toolmaker’s then-CEO, Donald Allan Jr., told shareholders that Stanley Black & Decker was preparing for the possibility. “Obviously, coming out of the gate, there would be price increases associated with tariffs that we put into the market,” he said during an earnings call.
